skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.description: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. //==================================================================================================
5. // Imports
6. //==================================================================================================
7. 
8. use vstd::prelude::*;
9. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
10. include!("number.spec.rs");
11. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
12. include!("number.proof.rs");
13. 
14. use crate::mem;
15. 
16. //==================================================================================================
17. // Structures
18. //==================================================================================================
19. 
20. ///
21. /// # Description
22. ///
23. /// A type that represents a frame number.
24. /// A frame number is in the range from `0` to [`Self::MAX`] (inclusive).
25. ///
26. #[verus_verify]
27. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
28. pub struct FrameNumber(usize);
29. 
30. //==================================================================================================
31. // Implementations
32. //==================================================================================================
33. 
34. #[verus_verify]
35. impl FrameNumber {
36.     /// The maximum frame number.
37.     ///
38.     /// This is the number of the highest frame whose entire extent fits within the addressable
39.     /// space `[0, MAX_ADDRESS]`. A frame `f` spans the byte range
40.     /// `[f * FRAME_SIZE, (f + 1) * FRAME_SIZE - 1]`, so the last fully-addressable frame is
41.     /// `(MAX_ADDRESS + 1) / FRAME_SIZE - 1`. That expression is rewritten below to avoid
42.     /// overflowing `usize` when `MAX_ADDRESS == usize::MAX`:
43.     ///
44.     /// - If `MAX_ADDRESS` is the last byte of its frame (`MAX_ADDRESS % FRAME_SIZE ==
45.     ///   FRAME_SIZE - 1`), that top frame is wholly addressable and is therefore the maximum.
46.     /// - Otherwise the top frame is only partially addressable, so the preceding frame is the
47.     ///   maximum.
48.     pub const MAX: usize = if mem::MAX_ADDRESS % mem::FRAME_SIZE == mem::FRAME_SIZE - 1 {
49.         mem::MAX_ADDRESS / mem::FRAME_SIZE
50.     } else {
51.         mem::MAX_ADDRESS / mem::FRAME_SIZE - 1
52.     };
53. 
54.     #[verus_spec(ensures Self::NULL@ == 0)]
55.     pub const NULL: Self = Self(0);
56. 
57.     ///
58.     /// # Description
59.     ///
60.     /// Constructs a [`FrameNumber`].
61.     ///
62.     /// # Parameters
63.     ///
64.     /// - `value`: The value of the frame number.
65.     ///
66.     /// # Returns
67.     ///
68.     /// - `Some(`[`FrameNumber`]`)`: Upon success.
69.     /// - `None`: If the value is greater than [`Self::MAX`].
70.     ///
71.     #[verus_spec(result =>
72.         ensures
73.             value as int <= Self::spec_max() ==> (result is Some
74.                 && (result->Some_0)@ == value as int),
75.             value as int > Self::spec_max() ==> result is None,
76.     )]
77.     pub fn from_raw_value(value: usize) -> Option<Self> {
78.         if value > Self::MAX {
79.             return None;
80.         }
81. 
82.         Some(Self(value))
83.     }
84. 
85.     ///
86.     /// # Description
87.     ///
88.     /// Converts a [`FrameNumber`] into a raw value.
89.     ///
90.     /// # Returns
91.     ///
92.     /// The raw value of the target [`FrameNumber`].
93.     ///
94.     #[verus_spec(result =>
95.         ensures
96.             result as int == self@,
97.             0 <= self@ <= Self::spec_max(),
98.     )]
99.     pub fn into_raw_value(self) -> usize {
100.         proof! { use_type_invariant(self); }
101.         self.0
102.     }
103. }
104. 
105. //==================================================================================================
106. // Unit Tests
107. //==================================================================================================
108. 
109. /// Tests if [`FrameNumber::from_raw_value()`] successfully constructs frame zero.
110. #[test]
111. fn test_frame_number_from_raw_value_zero() {
112.     let raw_value: usize = 0;
113.     let frame_number: FrameNumber = FrameNumber::from_raw_value(raw_value).unwrap();
114.     assert_eq!(frame_number.into_raw_value(), raw_value);
115. }
116. 
117. /// Tests if [`FrameNumber::from_raw_value()`] successfully constructs the maximum frame number.
118. #[test]
119. fn test_frame_number_from_raw_value_max() {
120.     let raw_value: usize = FrameNumber::MAX;
121.     let frame_number: FrameNumber = FrameNumber::from_raw_value(raw_value).unwrap();
122.     assert_eq!(frame_number.into_raw_value(), raw_value);
123. }
124. 
125. /// Regression test: the frame that contains the top-of-space address must be representable as a
126. /// [`FrameNumber`]. With an off-by-one [`FrameNumber::MAX`], converting such an address panicked.
127. #[test]
128. fn test_frame_number_top_of_space_is_representable() {
129.     // Frame number of the highest addressable byte.
130.     let top_frame: usize = mem::MAX_ADDRESS / mem::FRAME_SIZE;
131.     assert_eq!(FrameNumber::MAX, top_frame);
132.     assert!(FrameNumber::from_raw_value(top_frame).is_some());
133. }
134.

2. name: proof-extraction
3. description: "Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Proof Extraction
7. 
8. Extract large inline `proof { ... }` blocks from exec code into named lemmas
9. in the proof file (`<module>.proof.rs`).
10. 
11. ## Why
12. 
13. Large inline proof blocks hurt readability and make exec code hard to review.
14. Extracting them into lemmas with clear names documents *what* is being proven
15. and makes proofs reusable.
16. 
17. ## Tool
18. 
19. Use `check_proof_blocks` (MCP tool) or the CLI script to find blocks:
20. 
21. ```bash
22. python3 scripts/check_proof_blocks.py <source_file> --threshold 5 --all
23. ```
24. 
25. Output shows each proof block with its enclosing function, line range, and size.
26. Blocks marked `⚠️ EXTRACT` exceed the threshold.
27. 
28. ## Rules
29. 
30. | Block size  | Action |
31. |-------------|--------|
32. | >5 lines    | **Must** extract into a lemma in `.proof.rs` |
33. | 4-5 lines   | Extract if generic/reusable; keep if tightly coupled to exec context |
34. | 1-3 lines   | Keep inline |
35. 
36. ## Extraction Process
37. 
38. For each block to extract:
39. 
40. 1. Read the proof block and identify what it proves (the key `assert` / property).
41. 2. Create `proof fn lemma_<descriptive_name>` in `.proof.rs` with:
42.    - `requires`: the preconditions the proof depends on
43.    - `ensures`: the property being proven (must be strong enough for the call site)
44. 3. Replace the inline block with a 1-3 line lemma call.
45. 4. Run verification to confirm it still passes.
46. 
47. ## Loop Invariants
48. 
49. Long loop invariants (>5 clauses) also hurt readability. Factor out groups
50. of related clauses into named `spec fn` predicates:
51. 
52. ```rust
53. // Before: 10 invariant clauses inline
54. while i < n
55.     invariant
56.         0 <= i <= n,
57.         result.len() == i,
58.         forall|j: int| 0 <= j < i ==> result[j] == f(input[j]),
59.         ... // 7 more clauses
60. { ... }
61. 
62. // After: grouped into named predicates
63. spec fn loop_partial_result_ok(result: Seq<T>, input: Seq<T>, i: int) -> bool {
64.     result.len() == i
65.     && forall|j: int| 0 <= j < i ==> result[j] == f(input[j])
66. }
67. 
68. while i < n
69.     invariant
70.         0 <= i <= n,
71.         loop_partial_result_ok(result@, input@, i as int),
72.         ... // remaining clauses
73. { ... }
74. ```
75. 
76. Keep trivial bounds (`0 <= i <= n`) inline. Extract semantic groups
77. (data consistency, structural invariants) into named predicates.
78. 
79. ## Naming
80. 
81. Lemma names describe what they prove:
82. - ✅ `lemma_set_bit_preserves_inv`
83. - ✅ `lemma_alloc_range_bounded`
84. - ❌ `lemma_proof_block_1`
85. - ❌ `lemma_helper`
86. 
87. ## Constraints
88. 
89. - Do NOT change exec logic.
90. - Do NOT change spec function signatures.
91. - Verification must still pass after extraction.
92.

 in the proof file (`<module>.proof.rs`).

 ## Tool

 | Block size  | Action |
 |-------------|--------|
 | >5 lines    | **Must** extract into a lemma in `.proof.rs` |
 | 4-5 lines   | Extract if generic/reusable; keep if tightly coupled to exec context |
 | 1-3 lines   | Keep inline |

 For each block to extract:
 
 1. Read the proof block and identify what it proves (the key `assert` / property).
 2. Create `proof fn lemma_<descriptive_name>` in `.proof.rs` with:
    - `requires`: the preconditions the proof depends on
    - `ensures`: the property being proven (must be strong enough for the call site)
 3. Replace the inline block with a 1-3 line lemma call.

 ```rust
         result.len() == i,

     && forall|j: int| 0 <= j < i ==> result[j] == f(input[j])
 }
 
 while i < n
     invariant
         0 <= i <= n,
         loop_partial_result_ok(result@, input@, i as int),
         ... // remaining clauses
 { ... }
 ```

 (data consistency, structural invariants) into named predicates.

 Lemma names describe what they prove:
 - ✅ `lemma_set_bit_preserves_inv`
 - ✅ `lemma_alloc_range_bounded`
 - ❌ `lemma_proof_block_1`
 - ❌ `lemma_helper`

1. ---
2. name: proof-minimization
3. description: "Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity."
4. ---
5. 
6. # Proof Minimization
7. 
8. Remove redundant proof artifacts to make verification lean and readable
9. without weakening any guarantees.
10. 
11. ## What to Remove
12. 
13. 1. **Redundant lemmas** — another lemma proves the exact same property
14.    (same `requires` AND same `ensures`).
15. 2. **Redundant assertions** — `assert` statements that Verus can verify
16.    without them. Remove in bulk, then re-run verification.
17. 3. **Redundant proof hints** — unnecessary `by`, `by(nonlinear_arith)`,
18.    or trigger annotations that Verus doesn't need.
19. 4. **Dead spec functions** — non-public spec functions with zero callers (not
20.    referenced in any `requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`, or lemma). Keep
21.    `pub` spec functions — they may be part of the module's API for dependents.
22. 5. **Debug artifacts** — In spec/proof files: remove TODO comments, commented-out
23.    code, and property-ID annotations (e.g., `// FUNC-POST-3`, `// INV-2`). In
24.    exec files: remove unnecessary verification-related comments (e.g., obsolete
25.    proof hints, property-ID tags); do NOT remove original source comments.
26. 
27. ## What is NOT Redundant
28. 
29. - **Uncalled lemmas**: Verus verifies all lemmas regardless of callers.
30.   An uncalled lemma still proves a property. Only remove if another lemma
31.   proves the *exact* same thing.
32. - **Different preconditions**: Two lemmas with different `requires` prove
33.   different properties even if `ensures` looks similar.
34. 
35. **When in doubt, keep it.**
36. 
37. ## Process
38. 
39. This is a best-effort pass for readability, not an exhaustive search.
40. 
41. 1. **Assertions**: Remove `assert` statements that look redundant based on context.
42. 2. **Lemmas**: Remove a lemma only if another has identical `requires` + `ensures`.
43. 3. **Proof hints**: Remove `by(...)` annotations that look unnecessary.
44. 4. Re-run verification after changes — if it fails, revert the removal.
45. 
46. ## Constraints
47. 
48. - Do NOT add `assume`, `admit`, or `external_body`.
49. - Do NOT weaken any `ensures` or remove any meaningful property.
50. - Verification must pass after every removal batch.
51.
